what: Hamilton Lane helps institutions invest in private markets. It advises pension funds, insurers and sovereign wealth funds on where to commit money in private equity, private credit and infrastructure, runs funds that invest on their behalf, and sells the data and technology that underpin those decisions.
customers: Public and corporate pension funds, insurance companies, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, and increasingly wealthy individuals gaining access to private markets through intermediaries.
money: Fees on assets under management in its own funds and assets under advisement for consulting clients.
A share of investment gains once performance thresholds are met.
Subscription revenue from its private markets database and reporting platform.
moat: Private markets are opaque, and Hamilton Lane has decades of data on fund performance that nobody can replicate without having been there. That data makes its advice credible, which brings commitments, which generate more data. Institutional clients also stay for very long periods: changing a private markets adviser means disrupting a programme with commitments stretching a decade ahead.
risks: Only eight analysts cover the stock and they average $126.00 against an $84.98 price, a 48% gap that signals genuine disagreement rather than consensus.
Private markets fundraising has slowed considerably, which directly affects the fee-paying assets Hamilton Lane gathers.
Incentive fees depend on investment gains being realised, and exits in private equity have been slow, which delays them.
The shares trade at about 6.6 times sales, a premium that assumes the asset gathering resumes.
A prolonged period of poor private equity returns would damage both the fee base and the credibility of advising on the asset class.
opportunities: Revenue has more than doubled, from $367.9M in 2022 to $759.0M in 2026, which is strong growth for an asset manager.
A net margin of 32.8% and the shares at about 12.9 times earnings make this inexpensive relative to the growth.
Fee-paying assets are committed for a decade or more, which makes the revenue unusually predictable for an asset manager.
Access to private markets for wealthy individuals rather than only institutions is a large new channel where Hamilton Lane is early.
The data and technology business is a genuine asset: clients pay for information that cannot be assembled elsewhere.
watch: Fee-paying assets under management and the pace of new commitments. Revenue follows committed capital with a lag, so commitments tell you next year’s revenue before it appears.
view: Hamilton Lane sits in a better spot than the private equity firms it advises on. It does not need to generate investment returns to get paid; it gets paid for helping institutions decide where to commit and for managing the programmes that result. The fees are smaller than a general partner’s but the business is far more predictable, and the capital is committed for a decade or more, which makes the revenue base unusually durable for an asset manager.

The underappreciated asset is the data. Hamilton Lane has decades of fund-level performance information that nobody can assemble retrospectively, because it comes from having been in the room. That data makes the advice credible, the advice attracts commitments, and the commitments generate more data. It also supports a subscription business selling the information to people who want to underwrite private markets themselves. That is a compounding loop and it is the reason this is not simply a consulting firm.

Growth has been real — $368 million to $759 million of revenue in four years — and at 12.9 times earnings with a 32.8% net margin, the price does not reflect it. The reason, I think, is that private markets fundraising has slowed sharply: institutions are over-allocated to private equity, exits are slow, and distributions that would fund new commitments are not arriving. That affects Hamilton Lane directly, because its revenue follows commitments.

So the question is whether the slowdown is cyclical or structural, and I lean cyclical with one genuine caveat. The cyclical case is that the exit backlog clears, distributions resume, and institutions re-up. The caveat is that if private equity returns disappoint for a sustained period, both the fee base and the premise of advising on the asset class weaken together. The eight analysts at $126 against $85 are betting on the cyclical reading. Fee-paying assets and new commitments are the numbers that settle it, and they lead the revenue by roughly a year.
bull: Private markets fundraising resumes as exits clear, the individual-investor channel opens a large new source of commitments, and 13 times earnings on 33% margins rerates.
bear: Institutions stay over-allocated, private equity returns disappoint for years, and the fee base and the advisory premise weaken at the same time.
